newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE says no Serbia poll invite yet from Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: OSCE says no Serbia poll invite yet from Milosevic.

text.p: Europe's security forum, which sends observers to monitor elections, said on Friday it had not received a request from Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to send a delegation to Belgrade.

In a letter answering U.S. criticism of disputed local elections, Milosevic invited a delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) "to visit our country and be informed truthfully".
A spokeswoman for the Vienna-based forum said the OSCE could not react to the offer until it received a formal invitation from Belgrade authorities and studied the details.
"We have not received a formal request from Belgrade and until that time we cannot react to this in any way," the OSCE spokeswoman said.
"We would have to look at the invitation carefully and consider any conditions made in it," she added.
The United States has led Western attacks on Milosevic's refusal to accept opposition victories in local elections in Serbia on November 17.
The authorities overturned the results in Belgrade and other towns claimed by the opposition, citing unspecified "irregularities".
The conflict has provoked peaceful demonstrations drawing up to 150,000 people a day on to the streets of Belgrade. There have been reports of some protesters being detained and beaten.
Yugoslavia -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- had its membership of the OSCE suspended in 1992 after Belgrade was accused of stoking the war in neighbouring Bosnia.

The OSCE spokeswoman said there was no problem sending a delegation despite the suspension as long as an official request came from Belgrade. A team could be despatched immediately if OSCE officials believed the conditions were right.
But one Western diplomatic source said the OSCE should be very wary of any invitation from Milosevic and should tread carefully to avoid being manipulated by the Serbian president.

The full text of Milosevic's response to the United States published in Belgrade newspapers, claimed that opposition charges of socialist government vote-rigging had created a "distorted picture" internationally.
Milosevic has rejected all allegations of electoral fraud.
The source said it was highly unlikely an expert team of OSCE observers could in any way verify a vote which had taken place almost a month ago.
"Anything could have happened to the ballots in that time," the source said. "Checking the election in that way would serve no purpose."
If OSCE experts do decide to meet Milosevic, they may propose that the election should be re-run with a full team of OSCE observers to monitor the poll, a diplomatic source said.

This could possibly be a fave-saving option for the Serbian president, facing the biggest challenge to his nine-year rule from the demonstrations, which have also seen workers take to the streets for the first time this week.
